summary: Gives an overview of DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM), which lets an organization take responsibility for a message by signing it. It shows how DKIM fits into email services and how it relates to other message-signature technologies, for adopters, developers and deployers. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: DKIM lets an organisation sign an email message with a key it publishes in the DNS, so that the receiver can check that the message really came from that organisation and has not changed on the way. The memo explains how the pieces fit together and what such a signature does and does not prove.

questions: what does a dkim signature not do
subtitle: How DKIM lets an organisation sign a message and be checked on it.

tldr.problem: Email carries no reliable statement of who is responsible for a message, so a receiver has to judge each one on weak signals such as the sending IP address.
tldr.mechanism: DKIM lets a signer attach a signature to a message under a domain name it controls, publishes the matching public key in the DNS, and lets a receiver fetch that key and check the signature.
tldr.outcome: The document describes what a valid signature proves and, just as importantly, what it does not: it does not vouch for the From field, does not say what a receiver should do, and does not stop a verified message being sent again.

today: RFC 5585 is an Informational memo published in July 2009, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is an overview for those adopting, developing or deploying DKIM, and it points to RFC 4871 for the protocol itself and RFC 4686 for the threat analysis.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
DKIM allows an organisation to take responsibility for a message in a way a recipient can verify. The organisation can be a direct handler of the message, such as the author's, the originating sending site's, or an intermediary on the transit path, and it can also be an indirect handler such as an independent service helping a direct handler. It defines a domain-level digital signature authentication framework for email using public key cryptography, with the domain name service as its key server technology, as specified in RFC 4871.

The identifier used is a domain name, called the Signing Domain IDentifier, carried in the d= tag of the DKIM-Signature header field. The same identity can have several identifiers. Whoever signs chooses the identifier to use, and the owner of that domain is declaring that it accepts responsibility for the message and can be held accountable for it.

DKIM is a value-added feature. Mail that is not signed is handled exactly as it was before, and the document does not claim that DKIM solves the problems of spam, phishing, viruses or worms, calling it one basic tool in what needs to be a larger set. It sets out what a signature by itself does not do. It does not authenticate or verify the contents of the header or body, such as the From field, beyond certifying data integrity between signing and verifying. It makes no assertion about the behaviour of the signer. It prescribes no action for receivers to take on successful verification. It gives no protection after verification. And it does not protect against a message that already has a verified signature being sent again, so an intermediary or a recipient can repost a message with the original signature still verifiable even though the new recipients differ from those the author intended.

The document also reviews earlier work. The IP address of the sending system has traditionally been used as an identity, but it has security weaknesses and functional problems, and a domain name corresponds better to organisational boundaries. Four earlier IETF mail signature standards exist: PEM, first published in 1987; PGP, released in 1991 and later standardised as OpenPGP; MOSS, which PEM became in 1995; and S/MIME, developed independently by RSA Security. The document explains that DKIM differs by using an identifier specific to DKIM use, and by having the owner of the domain assert the validity of a key rather than having a third party attest to it. Keys are managed by adding records to the existing DNS, which avoids creating a new global infrastructure and reuses a service that is already efficient and reliable.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is simple: sign the message, publish the public key in the DNS, and let the receiver check the two against each other. The memo is careful to say what that check proves and what it does not.

sections.title: The Value DKIM Adds
sections.content:
The nature and origins of a message are often falsely stated, for legitimate or nefarious reasons. DKIM provides a foundation for distinguishing legitimate mail by associating a verifiable identifier with a message, so a receiver can decide how to handle it based on assessments of the identity behind the identifier.

Receiving services that verify a signature can use information about the signer as part of a programme to limit spam, spoofing, phishing and other unwanted behaviour. DKIM does not itself prescribe what a receiver should do; the services built on it typically do two things: determine a verified identity taking responsibility for the message, and evaluate how trustworthy that identity is. DKIM performs the first and enables the second.

On identity verification, the document notes that attackers can use a legitimate domain name, one they are not authorised to use, or a cousin name that looks like a legitimate one but is controlled by someone else. An assessment service using DKIM can tell a domain used by a known organisation from one used by others, so DKIM performs the positive step of identifying messages with verifiable identities rather than the negative step of finding messages with problematic use of an identity.

On trust assessments, a receiving service needs an accurate and stable identifier before it can use reputation information, otherwise the information may not pertain to the identified organisation's own actions. With an IP address the accuracy rests on the belief that the infrastructure supplies an accurate address; with a domain name some other verification is needed, and DKIM supplies it by declaring a valid responsible identity and using a digital signature to ensure that use of the identifier is authorised. A valid signature on its own neither lowers nor raises the trust attached to the message, but it lets other mechanisms do so. An organisation may publish information about its signing practices, which can let a receiver detect messages that claim to come from a domain but do not, and so reduce or leave unchanged its trust assessment.

On message validity, the cryptographic method gives certainty that a signed message, or the signed portion of it if the body is only partly signed, has not been modified between signing and verifying. If it was changed in any way, verification fails. This validity also neither raises nor lowers trust: a message that was untrustworthy when sent is certainly still untrustworthy when it verifies.
sections.plainLanguage: DKIM gives a receiver something it can rely on: a name that is tied to the message by a key the name's owner controls. The receiver can then judge that name by reputation, or by what the owner says about how it signs its mail.

sections.title: Goals and Design Choices
sections.content:
DKIM adds an end-to-end authentication capability to the existing mail transfer infrastructure. Because there can be many relaying hops between signing and verifying, the mechanism needs support only from the signer and the verifier, not from the components along the path.

The functional goals are these. Use domain-level granularity for assurance: DKIM provides accountability at the granularity of an organisation or department, and binds the signing key to a domain name, which also simplifies key management, allows the infrastructure rather than the user's mail program to sign, and reduces privacy concerns. This contrasts with OpenPGP and S/MIME, which associate verification with individual authors using their full email addresses. Keep the implementation local: any party anywhere along the transit path can sign, and a message can carry more than one signature. Allow signing to be delegated to independent parties: a party may sign with any domain name for which it holds authorised keys, which supports an organisation that outsources part of its processing, and a reputation provider can delegate a key for a domain it controls to an organisation it vouches for. Distinguish the core mechanism from its uses: the only semantics inherent in a DKIM signature are that the signer asserts some kind of responsibility for the message. Any interpretation of that responsibility belongs to services built on DKIM. And retain the ability to have anonymous email: DKIM permits authentication of the mail system operator rather than the author, so a message that definitely came from a domain does not threaten the anonymity of the person who wrote it.

The operational goals are equally explicit. The presence of a signature must be transparent to recipients that do not support it, and unlike S/MIME and OpenPGP, DKIM does not modify the message body. A signature that fails verification must be treated exactly as if no signature were present, so that the message reverts to normal handling through the receiver's existing filters; OpenPGP and S/MIME were designed to treat verification failure as message failure. Incremental adoption must give incremental benefit: any two organisations that exchange mail can use DKIM without the rest of the Internet adopting it, and the benefits grow with adoption. The amount of required infrastructure must be small, which the reliance on the DNS achieves. And a wide range of deployment choices must be allowed: DKIM can be deployed in various places within an organisation's mail service, such as an outbound boundary transfer agent, which would mean internal mail is not signed at all.
sections.plainLanguage: The design choices all point one way: DKIM should not change how mail works for anyone who ignores it. A broken signature is treated as no signature, the message body is untouched, and the only new infrastructure is a DNS record.

sections.title: How DKIM Signs and Verifies
sections.content:
Signing works like this. The signer chooses a Signing Domain IDentifier, performs digital signing on the message, and adds the signature information in a DKIM-Signature header field. A verifier takes the domain name and the selector from that header field, obtains the public key associated with that name, and verifies the signature. DKIM permits any domain name to be used as the identifier and supports extensible choices of algorithm, with a core set of algorithms that all implementations must support so that basic interoperability is guaranteed. A key can also be restricted to signing messages for particular types of service, such as a single source of mail, which helps when signing authority is delegated to a department or to an outsourced service. The signer explicitly lists the header fields that are signed, such as From, Date and Subject, and by choosing the smallest set needed the signature is more robust against the handling vagaries of intermediary transfer agents.

A DKIM signature applies to the message body and to the selected header fields. The signer computes a hash of the selected header fields and another hash of the body, then uses a private key to encode that information along with the other signing parameters, and places the result in the new DKIM-Signature message header field.

The key for a signature is associated with the Signing Domain IDentifier, and that domain name is the complete identity used for assessments about the signer, although the specification gives no guidance on how to make an assessment. The name alone is not enough to look up the key in the DNS, because one domain may have several signing keys or several potential signers. DKIM therefore identifies a particular signature by the combination of the domain and an added field called the selector, given as a separate parameter of the DKIM-Signature header field. The semantics of the selector are reserved to the signer and are to be treated as an opaque string by everyone else: if verifiers used the selector in an assessment, there would be no way left to move from an old or compromised key to a new one.

Verification can be performed by any agent in the transit path, and message recipients can verify by querying the DNS for the signer's domain to retrieve the public key, which confirms that the message was signed by a party holding the private key for that domain. Verification is typically done by an agent in the administrative management domain of the recipient.

Signers that need several independent assessments of their own organisation can use different sub-domains as the identifier, such as transaction.example.com against newsletter.example.com, and these can be entirely separate from the domain in the From header field.
sections.plainLanguage: The signer hashes the headers it lists and the body, and signs those hashes with a private key. The verifier looks up the matching public key in the DNS and checks the signature against it. The selector is what lets one domain publish several keys at once.

sections.title: Service Architecture
sections.content:
Basic processing is divided between a signing administrative management domain and a verifying one. At the simplest this is the originating domain and the delivering domain, but other domains on the handling path can be involved. Signing is performed by an authorised module in the signing domain using private information from the key store; within the originating domain this might be the mail user agent, the submission agent or a transfer agent. Verification is performed by an authorised module in the verifying domain, which might be a transfer agent, a delivery agent or a user agent. It verifies the signature or determines whether a signature was required, using public information from the key store. If the signature passes, reputation information is used to assess the signer and passed to the message filtering system. If it fails, or there is no signature under the author's domain, information about the signing practices related to the author can be retrieved remotely or held locally and passed to the filtering system. When a message has more than one valid signature, the order in which signers are assessed and the interactions among those assessments are not defined by the specification.

Several tables and services provide the external information, each adding administration and maintenance. The key store holds the keys: the signing organisation needs a way to add a key to the DNS for every selector and domain combination, and policies for distributing and revising keys. Reputation and accreditation information, associated with a domain name, comes in many forms and from many sources; DKIM does not define assessment services, and its relevance to them is to supply a verified domain name to assess. Signing practices are separate from both signature validity and reputation: they say how a domain is used, such as whether it signs mail at all, whether all mail bearing that domain in the From field is signed, or whether the owner recommends discarding unsigned mail. They are made at the level of a domain name, are distinct from assessments about particular messages, and any checking of them is optional and a matter of local policy.

The document expects the common place for an implementation to be the outbound service of the authoring organisation and the inbound service of the receiving organisation, such as a department or a boundary transfer agent; implementing it in a user's mail program is expected to be less typical because it costs more to administer and support. A mediator, which is a delivery agent that can repost a modified message, such as a mailing list, can let a signature survive some modifications and can add a signature of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing happens in one organisation's mail system and checking in another's, with the DNS in between holding the keys. Everything else, such as reputation and filtering, sits outside DKIM and uses the verified name it produces.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document states that the security considerations of the DKIM protocol are described in the DKIM base specification, RFC 4871, with RFC 4686 as their basis. It does not restate them, and it also says that it does not provide information on threats to DKIM or to email, or details of the protocol, which are in those two documents.
sections.plainLanguage: This overview does not cover the attacks DKIM is designed against. Those are set out in the DKIM specification itself and in the threat analysis it points to.

messages.label: SIGNED MESSAGE
messages.note: The DKIM-Signature header field carries the signature, the domain identifier and the selector.

messages.label: KEY QUERY
messages.note: The verifier looks up the public key named by the selector and the domain.

messages.label: PUBLIC KEY
messages.note: The verifier checks the signature with the returned key and passes the result to the filtering system.

viz.caption: WHAT A DKIM SIGNATURE ON ITS OWN DOES NOT DO

items.title: No claim about the From field
items.text: It certifies only that the signed data has not changed between signing and verifying.

items.title: No claim about the signer
items.text: A valid signature says nothing about how the signer behaves.

items.title: No instruction to receivers
items.text: DKIM prescribes no action for a receiver to take after a successful verification.

items.title: No protection afterwards
items.text: Nothing protects a message once it has been verified.

items.title: No protection against replay
items.text: A message with a valid signature can be sent on again and the signature still verifies.

viz.caption: DKIM AGAINST THE EARLIER MAIL SIGNATURE SCHEMES

cells: An organisation, by its domain name
An individual author, by full email address
Certificates, or a web of trust
Only a new header field; the body is untouched
The message is treated as if it were unsigned
The message is treated as failed
